title: Geopolitics: Russia votes under a drone barrage, Gulf states seek a security framework, and Canada leans toward Europe
summary: Ukraine's largest drone attack on Moscow landed on the final day of Russia's parliamentary election, while Qatar's prime minister described the fallout of the US-Israel war on Iran as an earthquake and pressed for a Gulf security framework with Tehran. Elsewhere, eighteen suspects were extradited over the 2021 killing of Haiti's president, France and Canada moved to deepen ties, Germany's chancellor called a state election a disaster for his party, Michelle Bachelet quit the UN leadership race and a Greenland security deal was welcomed by NATO.

stories.headline: Largest attack on Moscow sees Ukraine fire hundreds of drones, mayor says
stories.dek: The barrage described as the largest on the Russian capital landed on the final day of Russia's parliamentary vote, as Moscow also moved to protect its rail network.
tldr: Moscow's mayor said the city faced the largest attack of the war, with hundreds of Ukrainian drones fired at the capital, according to BBC reporting.
The strike came on the final day of Russia's parliamentary election, which the Kremlin has framed as a measure of support for the war.
DW reported that Russia's vote unfolded amid war fatigue and anxiety, and that Ukraine has stepped up measures to protect its railways.

body.text: Moscow's mayor said the Russian capital came under the largest attack of the war, with Ukraine firing hundreds of drones toward the city, according to BBC reporting. The item is carried at headline level and does not include casualty or interception figures.

The timing placed the attack on the third and final day of Russia's parliamentary election. DW described a war-fatigued and anxious country picking a new parliament, framing the vote as a test of domestic sentiment rather than a competitive contest.

Both sides have hardened their infrastructure defenses. DW reported that Ukraine is stepping up measures to protect its railways, days after the US signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill that also targets the shadow tanker fleet moving Russian energy.

stories.whyItMatters: Strikes reaching the Russian capital in volume, on election day, show Ukraine's long-range drone campaign now touches Russia's political core in single nights while both sides harden the infrastructure the war runs on.
stories.editorNote: The drone figures and the election-day framing come from wire headlines across BBC and DW; the collection does not include detailed strike assessments, so the extent of damage is not asserted.

stories.headline: US, China open high-level talks ahead of Trump-Xi summit
stories.dek: Trade and technology are back on the table as Washington and Beijing open talks before a planned leaders' meeting.
tldr: US and Chinese officials opened high-level talks ahead of a planned Trump-Xi summit, according to Al Jazeera.
The Guardian reported that China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development, a dispute running in parallel with the economic agenda.
The collection carries the talks at headline level, without the specific negotiating positions on either side.

body.text: The United States and China opened high-level talks ahead of a planned summit between their leaders, Al Jazeera reported. The meeting is framed as preparation for a Trump-Xi encounter rather than a conclusion in itself.

Technology is a live fault line in the relationship. The Guardian reported on why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development, a disagreement that sits alongside trade in the run-up to the summit.

stories.whyItMatters: A leaders' summit would set the tone for trade, critical minerals and AI governance at once. Pre-summit talks and an open dispute over AI framing indicate the agenda is economic and technological together.
stories.editorNote: Wire headlines only; no negotiating positions, dates for the summit or deliverables are asserted because they are not in the collection.

stories.headline: Qatar PM describes fallout of US-Israel war on Iran as ‘earthquake’
stories.dek: Doha pressed for a Gulf security framework with Tehran and offered to revive Iran-US talks, as Houthi missile fire on Saudi Arabia and allied hesitation widened the region's fault lines.
tldr: Qatar's prime minister described the fallout of the US-Israel war on Iran as an earthquake and warned against cycles of escalation, Al Jazeera reported.
He urged a Gulf security framework with Iran and said Qatar is working to revive Iran-US talks.
The Houthis said they targeted the Saudi capital with ballistic missiles, and South Korea said it would not send military support for the US campaign against Iran.

body.text: Qatar's prime minister described the fallout of the US-Israel war on Iran as an earthquake and warned against further cycles of escalation in the Middle East, according to Al Jazeera. The framing places Doha among the regional states most exposed to any widening of the conflict.

Diplomacy is the counterweight. Al Jazeera reported that the Qatari premier urged a Gulf security framework with Iran and said Qatar is working to revive Iran-US talks, positioning the emirate as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran.
The military track kept moving. The Houthis said they targeted the Saudi capital with ballistic missiles, and DW assessed how powerful the group has become as the confrontation with Riyadh widens.
Allied participation is not guaranteed. The Guardian reported that South Korea will not send military forces to support the US war on Iran, defying pressure from President Trump.

stories.whyItMatters: The Gulf is trying to manage two tracks at once: containing escalation with Iran and keeping the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi energy infrastructure out of the crossfire. Doha's mediation offer and Seoul's refusal show the coalition around the campaign is not uniform.
stories.editorNote: The Qatar items are wire reports of statements, not agreements; the Houthi claim and the missile attack are reported as claimed, without independent damage assessment in the collection.

stories.headline: Eighteen suspects extradited to US over Haitian president’s 2021 killing
stories.dek: A long-running investigation into the assassination of President Jovenel Moise produced a fresh wave of extraditions and arrests.
tldr: Eighteen suspects were extradited to the United States over the 2021 killing of Haiti's president, Al Jazeera reported.
The Guardian reported that more than a dozen people were arrested in connection with the assassination.
The two reports describe the same case from different stages of the process, and the collection does not include charges or court dates.

body.text: Eighteen suspects were extradited to the United States over the 2021 killing of Haitian president Jovenel Moise, Al Jazeera reported. The Guardian, covering the same investigation, reported that more than a dozen people had been arrested in connection with the assassination.

stories.whyItMatters: The Moise killing destabilized Haitian politics and became a test of cross-border prosecution. A large extradition to the United States signals the case is still moving through the legal system years later.
stories.editorNote: Both items are headline-level wire reports; the collection does not include the identities of those extradited, the charges, or the jurisdictions involved beyond the US.

stories.headline: France’s Macron and Canada’s Carney announce plans to build stronger ties
stories.dek: Paris and Ottawa moved to deepen their relationship as Canada weighs a closer role with the European Union.
tldr: France's president and Canada's prime minister announced plans to build stronger ties, Al Jazeera reported.
DW examined the European Union's special relationships, and The Guardian reported that uncertainty clouds Canada's EU membership plan despite a warm reception in Strasbourg.
The items describe intent and process, not a concluded agreement.

body.text: President Emmanuel Macron of France and Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada announced plans to build stronger ties, Al Jazeera reported. The announcement came as Canada deepens its engagement with Europe.

The broader frame is Canada's relationship with the European Union. DW surveyed the bloc's special relationships, while The Guardian reported that Canada's EU membership plan remains clouded by uncertainty despite an amicable reception in Strasbourg.

stories.whyItMatters: Canada's turn toward Europe is a hedge against trade exposure to the United States. Whether it becomes formal EU integration or a set of bilateral deals will shape North Atlantic economic alignment.
stories.editorNote: These are political announcements and analysis, not a signed agreement; the collection has no terms, timeline or membership mechanism.
